slides: Let's continue with the chart page.

slides.say: So what do we do when the example doesn't match what we see?
We stop. We don't go on to the questions yet, because if we don't understand the example, we don't understand the chart.
We read the explanation again, slowly, line by line. Then we check the example again.

slides: Now it's clear? Excellent, we go to the questions.

slides.say: Still not clear? Then we leave the set for now. We solve the rest of the section, and we come back to the chart at the end.

slides: That way we don't waste time on questions about a chart we don't understand.

slides.say: Now the chart itself. We look at its title, and at the units on the axes.
Is the number in thousands, in hundreds, or in percent? For example, ninety on a thousands axis means ninety thousand.
And forty on a percent axis means forty percent. It's not forty people.
Then we read every note under the chart. A note is there for a reason. Without it, something won't add up.
at: A note is there for a reason

slides.say: After the chart come the questions. They go from easy to hard.
at: After the chart come the questions

slides.say: So the first question is the easiest, and the last is the hardest. The last one can be harder, or just longer to calculate.
The first question usually checks one thing. Do we understand the chart? It asks us to read one value from the chart.
at: read one value from the chart

slides.say: For example, how many vehicles were sold in two thousand eleven? We read eighty thousand, and that's it.
The later questions go further. Some need a calculation, and some need a deeper understanding of the chart.
The chart set has a place in the section too. And its place tells us how hard it is.
A set at the start of the section is easy. A set at the end is hard.

slides: You may hear this advice, always skip the chart, and come back to it at the end. That's a mistake.
Here's why. A chart at the start is not only easy. It's usually easier than the other questions around it.

slides.say: Let's say students answer eighty percent of the first questions right. Then they answer about eighty-five percent of the chart questions right.
So a chart at the start, or in the middle, we solve when we get to it.
A chart at the end, we reach at the end anyway. So there's nothing to skip.

slides: If charts are really hard for you, you may choose to skip them. But for most students, an early chart is worth solving. [pause] Okay. I'll see you in the next part.
